blocks.text: Satellites are objects that orbit in nearly circular path around the Earth. They are put into orbit by rockets and are held in orbits by the gravitational pull of the Earth. The low flying Earth satellites have acceleration 9.8 m s⁻² towards the centre of the Earth. If there is no gravitational pull, they would fly off in a straight line along tangent to the orbit. When the satellite is moving in a circle, it has an acceleration v²/r. In a circular orbit around the Earth, the centripetal acceleration is supplied by gravity and we have

blocks.text: Newton had predicated about the artificial satellites 300 years ago. The above figure has been taken from his well-known book “Principia Mathematica”. According to this book, if an object is thrown horizontally with a particular speed from a place which is sufficiently high, it will start revolving around the Earth.

blocks.text: If, however, a satellite in a circular orbit is at a distance h much greater than R above the Earth's surface, we must take into account the experimental fact that the gravitational acceleration decreases inversely as the square of the distance from the centre of the Earth (Fig. 3.11).

blocks.alt: The Earth, of radius R, on the left; a double arrow R runs from its centre to its surface. Far to the right a satellite sits on an arc of its orbit, with an arrow v along the orbit. A double arrow h runs from the Earth's surface to the satellite, and the note h >> R is printed below the Earth.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.11: A satellite at a height h much greater than the Earth's radius R (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.11).

blocks.text: The higher the satellite, the slower will be the required speed and longer it will take to complete one revolution around the Earth.
